suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))

Components of the model
See (2020, pp. 32–35).
\[ Pr(W,L|p)=\frac{(W+L)!}{W!L!}p^W(1-p)^L  \tag{1}\]
The probability of \(W\) and \(L\), conditional on \(p\) is defined by the formula in Equation 1.
The dbinom() function computes this binomial probability. To compute the probability of observing \(x=6\) \(W\)s in 9 globe tosses with \(p=4\), we proceed as indicated below:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
dbinom(x = 6, size = 9, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE)
```

[1] 0.1640625


So, to compute the binomial probabilities for observing all \(n+1\) possible cases, we proceed as follows:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_W <- 0:9
p_n <- purrr::map(n_W, dbinom, size = 9, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_1 <- data.frame(n_obs = n_W, p_n = p_n)

# Plot the data
like_1 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = n_obs, y = p_n)) +
  theme_classic()
```








To produce a set of binomial plots based on increasing numbers of samples, we proceed as follows.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_samples <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

how_many_W <- function(n) 0:n
n_W <- purrr::map(n_samples, how_many_W) |>
  purrr::list_c()

n_states <- rep(n_samples, n_samples+1)

p_n <- purrr::map2(n_W, n_states, dbinom, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_2 <- data.frame(n_states = n_states, n_W = n_W, p_n = p_n)
```



Code
like_2 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = n_W, y = p_n)) +
  facet_wrap(n_states, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle("Probability density as number of samples increases.")









So, this figure isn’t quite what I want. But it’s a start. What I think I want is a graph that plots the proportion of times \(W\) was picked out of \(n\) samples vs. the probability density.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_samples <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

how_many_W <- function(n) 0:n
n_W <- purrr::map(n_samples, how_many_W) |>
  purrr::list_c()

n_states <- rep(n_samples, n_samples+1)

p_W <- n_W/n_states

p_n <- purrr::map2(n_W, n_states, dbinom, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_3 <- data.frame(n_states = n_states, n_W = n_W, p_W = p_W, p_n = p_n)
```



Code
like_3 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = p_W, y = p_n)) +
  facet_wrap(n_states, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle("Probability density for a given proportion of W's as number of samples increases.")









Yes. That’s it.

# Better to make a function

# Helper function
plot_posterior <- function(n_W = 3, n = 3, prior_p = 1) {
  if (n_W > n) error("n_W must be <= n.")
  
  prior <- rep(prior_p, n)
  p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n)
  likelihood <- dbinom(x = n_W, size = n, prob = p_grid)
  unstd.posterior <- likelihood*prior
  posterior <- unstd.posterior/sum(unstd.posterior)
  plot(x = p_grid, y = posterior, type = "b")
}

Ex 2M2
Create a function to compute p_prior.


Code
compute_p_prior <- function(n = 10, p_const = .5) {
  p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
  p[p < p_const] <- 0
  p[p >= p_const] <- p_const
  p
}

compute_p_prior()

plot_posterior_2 <- function(n_W = 3, n = 3, p_const = 0.5) {

  unstd.posterior <- likelihood*prior

  p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
  p[p < p_thresh] <- 0
  p[p >= p_thresh] <- p_const
  p
}

plot_posterior_2 <- function(obs = c("W", "W", "W"), n = length(obs), 
                             p_thresh = 0.5, p_const = 0.7) {
  
  n_W = sum(obs == "W")
  prior <- compute_p_prior_2(n, p_const, p_thresh)
  p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n)
  
  likelihood <- dbinom(x = n_W, size = n, prob = p_grid)
  unstd.posterior <- likelihood*prior
  posterior <- unstd.posterior/sum(unstd.posterior)
  
  plot(x = p_grid, y = posterior, type = "b",
       xlab = "prob of water",
       ylab = "posterior probability")
}

Ex 2M3
Let’s create a generative model.
A toss consists of two data elements, the unknown planet (Mars or Earth), and the observed observation of land.
So, we want to determine the following:
\[p(Earth|land)\] This implies the following:
\[p(Earth|land) \propto p(land|Earth)*p(Earth)\]
Or, exactly
\[p(Earth|land) = \frac{p(land|Earth)*p(Earth)}{p(land)}\]
We know that
\[p(land|Earth)=1-0.7=0.3\], and
\[p(Earth)=0.5\]. We also know that
\[p(land|Mars)=1\]
and \[p(Mars)=0.5\].
We can compute \(p(land)\) as follows:
\[p(land)=p(land|Earth)*p(Earth)+p(land|Mars)*p(Mars)\]
or \[0.3*0.5+1*.5 =\]
0.65
So,
\[p(Earth|land) = \frac{p(land|Earth)*p(Earth)}{p(land)}\]
is \[\frac{0.3*0.5}{0.65}=0.23\]

rw <- function(steps = 1, n = 50) {
  df <- data.frame(trajectory = 1:n, step = rep(0, n), pos = rep(0, n))
  this_df <- df
  for (i in 1:steps) {

Now, here’s a version that uses a function.


Code
est_p_water <- function(obs, p = 0.5, n_pts = 20) {
    assertthat::assert_that(is.character(obs))
    assertthat::is.number(p)
    assertthat::assert_that(p > 0 & p <= 1)
    assertthat::is.number(n_pts)
    assertthat::assert_that(n_pts > 0)

    p.grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n_pts)
    prior <- rep(p, n_pts)
    n_W <- sum(obs == "W")
    likelihood <- dbinom(n_W, size = length(obs), prob = p.grid)
    posterior.unstd <- likelihood * prior
    posterior <- posterior.unstd / sum(posterior.unstd)
    m_comment <- paste0(
        n_W,
        " water observations out of ",
        length(obs),
        " | ",
        n_pts,
        " points"
    )
    plot(
        p.grid,
        posterior,
        type = "b",
        xlab = "probability of water",
        ylab = "posterior probability"
    )
    mtext(m_comment)
}

We need to modify our function slightly.

est_p_water_2 <- function(obs, p = 0.5, n_pts = 20) {
  assertthat::assert_that(is.character(obs))
  assertthat::is.number(p)
  assertthat::assert_that(p > 0 & p <= 1)
  assertthat::is.number(n_pts)
  assertthat::assert_that(n_pts > 0)

  p.grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n_pts)
  prior <- ifelse(p.grid < p, 0, p)
  n_W <- sum(obs == "W")
  likelihood <- dbinom(n_W, size = length(obs), prob = p.grid)
  posterior.unstd <- likelihood * prior
  posterior <- posterior.unstd / sum(posterior.unstd)
  m_comment <- paste0(
    n_W,
    " water observations out of ",
    length(obs),
    " | ",
    n_pts,
    " points"
  )
  plot(
    p.grid,
    posterior,
    type = "b",
    xlab = "probability of water",
    ylab = "posterior probability"
  )
  mtext(m_comment)
}

PM3. Two globes, Earth with p(Water)=0.70 and Mars with p(Water)=0.
We want to compute \(p(Earth|land)\).
\(p(Earth|land)=\frac{p(land|Earth)p(Earth)}{p(land)}\)
\(p(land|Earth)=0.30\) \(p(land|Mars)=1.0\) \(p(Earth)=0.5\) \(p(land)=0.5*p(land|Earth)+0.5*p(land|Mars)\)


Code
p_land_Earth <- 0.30
p_land_Mars <- 1
p_Earth <- 0.5
p_land <- p_Earth * (p_land_Earth) + (1 - p_Earth) * p_land_Mars

p_Earth_land <- (p_land_Earth * p_Earth) / p_land
p_Earth_land


[1] 0.2307692




2M4. Card deck with three cards.
\(c_{bb}\rightarrow{b,b}\) \(c_{bw}\rightarrow{b,w}\) \(c_{ww}\rightarrow{w,w}\)
There are two events. One involves the choice of card, the other involves the choice of side. So, the space of possible outcomes when the observer chooses one card is as follows:
\(b,b,b,w,w,w\)
\(c_{bb}\) could produce the observed data (black side up) in 2 ways. \(c_{bw}\) could produce the observed data in one way. \(c_{ww}\) could not produce the observed data, so there are zero ways.
So, there are three ways the observed data could be produced. In two of the ways, the other side is black. Thus, \(p(other-side-black|observed)=2/3\)


2H1. Pandas.
\(p(twin|A)=.1\) \(p(twin|B)=.2\)
We observe a panda who gives birth to twins, what is the probability that the next birth will also be twins? Species is unknown.
Species unknown and likely sampled in equal proportions means that \(p(A)=p(B)=0.5\)
Species A could generate the observed first birth in 1/10 ways. Species B could generate the observed first birth in 2/10 ways. We want the probability of observing two consecutive twin births, \(p(twin*twin)\).
\(p(twin*twin)=p(twin*twin|A)p(A)+p(twin*twin|B)p(B)\) \(p(twin*twin)=p(twin|A)*p(twin|A)*p(A)+p(twin|B)p(twin|B)*p(B)\)


Code
p_twin_A <- 0.1
p_twin_B <- 0.2
p_A <- 0.5

p_twin_twin <- p_twin_A * p_twin_A * p_A + p_twin_B * p_twin_B * (1 - p_A)
p_twin_twin


[1] 0.025


So, the probability that the next birth will be a twin, given that the first was a twin, $p(twin,twin)=$0.025.


2H2. More pandas
What is the probability that the species is A, given that the first birth is a pair of twins? In other words, what is \(p(A|twin)\)?
\(p(A|twin)=\frac{p(twin|A)*p(A)}{p(twin)}\)
\(p(twin)=p(twin|A)*p(A)+p(twin|B)*p(B)\)


Code
p_twin <- p_twin_A * p_A + p_twin_B * (1 - p_A)




Code
p_A_twin <- (p_twin_A * p_A) / p_twin
p_A_twin


[1] 0.3333333


So, \(p(A|twin)\)=0.3333333.

title: Gilmore rethinks
text:
I ran across McElreath’s book (2020) and YouTube video series (Statistical rethinking 2023, 2023) by accident.
But Pasteur said that “fortune favors the prepared mind” (“Louis pasteur,” 2004). So, I acknowledge that I have enjoyed these materials in large part because I was looking for something like them. Specifically, I’ve recommended simulation and visualization as vital data analytic techniques without really appreciating how these ideas mesh with Bayesian approaches. I find myself generating directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) without appreciating their utility in data analyses. And, I have read, but only partially grasped the ideas in Judea Pearl’s work on causal modeling (Mackenzie & Pearl, 2020; Pearl, 2009).
This site represents my notes and comments on the textbook and the video series as I work my way through them. By creating code, equations, and visualizations, I hope to master the material and add some new Quarto tricks to my toolkit.
